414.title: Show me one
414.hook: show me someone ill and happy, in danger and happy: show me a Stoic (Discourses 2.19)
414.howItsDone: Some readers of Epictetus judge their practice less by what they know about Stoicism than by how they act on an ordinary hard day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was orgē, anger, and the count of calm days. Your line was give the anger nothing to burn.

Somebody at a party explains, in great detail, the whole theory of mindfulness. Five minutes later they're furious at the bartender. The theory was flawless. The bartender saw none of it. Knowing the words is one thing; living them is another. Epictetus had students who could talk their way through Stoic arguments with ease. In one talk he turns on them, and asks for something no amount of reciting could fake.
screen: `THE WHOLE THEORY OF MINDFULNESS.` → `FURIOUS AT THE BARTENDER.` → `SOMETHING RECITING CAN'T FAKE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter nineteen. It opens with a famous puzzle in logic, the Master Argument, and the people who show off by discussing it. Epictetus lets them talk, and then turns. You can all recite the arguments, he says. So who among you is a Stoic? We call a statue Phidian when it's shaped by Phidias' art. Show me a person shaped by the beliefs they talk about. Then the list. Show me someone who is sick, and happy. In danger, and happy. Dying, and happy. Exiled, and happy. Disgraced, and happy. Show me! By the gods, he says, I long to see a Stoic. Then he does something disarming. He lowers the bar. You can't show me one who's finished, he admits. Then show me one who's being shaped, who has started leaning that way. Do an old man a favor. Don't keep from me a sight I've never yet seen. Sit with that. A Stoic teacher says he has never yet seen a finished Stoic. That's not despair. It's the honesty that keeps the whole thing real. Nobody here is finished. The question is only whether you're being shaped, whether someone watching you on a hard day could see the arguments turning into a person. Not the whole statue. One recognizable line of it.

415.title: No scorekeeping
415.hook: only those who place good in the will can truly be friends (Discourses 2.22)
415.howItsDone: Some readers of this chapter check their friendships for a hidden ledger, and practice acts of friendship with nothing expected back.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Master Argument, and the Stoic Epictetus longed to see. Your line was one who's being shaped.

Two puppies are tumbling around on the rug, licking each other's faces, best friends. Now drop a piece of meat between them. In about half a second you'll see what the friendship was made of. The licking stops. The growling starts. Whatever the friendship was, it didn't survive one piece of meat. Epictetus used exactly that picture, and then he dropped other things between people: a piece of land, a throne.
screen: `TWO PUPPIES ON THE RUG.` → `DROP A PIECE OF MEAT.` → `A FIELD, A THRONE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter twenty-two, on friendship. Epictetus starts with a simple claim: we love what we think is good. So who can really be a friend? Only someone who knows what's actually good. Then the dogs: throw meat between them and you'll see. Then people. Throw a field between a father and a son, and see how fast the son wants his father gone, and the father the son. He reaches for an old story: Eteocles and Polynices, two brothers in Greek legend who fought over the throne of Thebes and, as the legend tells it, killed each other. They'd been raised together, eaten and drunk together, slept under one roof. The throne fell between them like the meat. His diagnosis: wherever a person puts their I and their mine, that's where they lean. If my good is in money, your money is always a little bit against me. If my good is in being admired, your success is a threat. That's when friends start keeping score: who called whom, who paid last, who got the better job. But if my good is in my own will, in being honest and kind and faithful, nothing that falls between us can turn you into a rival. You can't steal my honesty by getting the promotion. That, Epictetus says, is the only ground a lasting friendship can stand on: two people who've placed their good where no piece of meat can land.

416.title: Real beauty
416.hook: to a young man with elaborate hair: beauty is in excellence, not in grooming (Discourses 3.1)
416.carry: you're your will, your choosing self
416.howItsDone: Some readers of this chapter make a point of praising others for their character rather than their appearance, and give their own mornings to character as well as grooming.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was no scorekeeping: put your good in your will, and nothing that falls between friends makes them rivals. Your line was nothing to keep score of.

A young student of public speaking came to the Stoic teacher Epictetus with his hair dressed more elaborately than usual, his whole appearance polished to a shine. Should a teacher say something? Epictetus weighs it. If I keep quiet, he reasons, this young man may someday say: Epictetus saw me like that, and never said a word. So he speaks. But he doesn't mock. He asks a question about dogs and horses.
screen: `HAIR DRESSED WITH GREAT CARE.` → `SHOULD HE SAY SOMETHING?` → `A QUESTION ABOUT DOGS.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter one. Tell me, Epictetus says to the young man, don't you think some dogs are beautiful? Some horses? Yes. Is it the same thing that makes each of them beautiful, or something different? A dog is beautiful when it's excellent as a dog, a horse when it's excellent as a horse. A beautiful racehorse and a beautiful sheepdog aren't beautiful in the same way; each is beautiful by being very good at being what it is. So what makes a human being beautiful? Excellence as a human. And what is that? Justice. Moderation. Self-control. If you want to be beautiful, Epictetus tells him, work on those. Then comes the line that turns a lecture into a kindness. You aren't your hair, he says, or your skin. You're your will, your choosing self. Make that beautiful, and you will be beautiful. He's not against looking after yourself. Elsewhere in the Discourses he's quite firm that students should keep clean and not put people off. His point is about where the real work goes. A morning in front of the mirror shapes the hair. A morning of being honest, patient and fair shapes the person. Only one of those, for Epictetus, is the beauty that belongs to a human being.

417.title: Three fields
417.hook: desire, action and assent: the three areas of training (Discourses 3.2)
417.carry: let each door open for a few breaths
417.howItsDone: Many modern Stoic practitioners organize their practice around Epictetus' three fields, sometimes focusing on one per day: desire, action or assent.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was real beauty: a human's excellence is justice and self-control. Your line was you're your will, your choosing self.

A good gym program doesn't just say get fit. It splits the work: one day legs, one day upper body, one day endurance. You know what you're training today, and why. A few weeks ago, back on not more books, Epictetus told a proud student to show him his progress in desire, action and judgment. Now, at the start of book three of the Discourses, he lays out that plan in full: three fields, in order, with a warning about which one people skip to first.
screen: `LEGS, UPPER BODY, ENDURANCE.` → `DESIRE, ACTION, JUDGMENT.` → `THE ONE PEOPLE SKIP TO.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter two. There are three fields, Epictetus says, in which anyone who wants to be good has to train. The first is desire and aversion: learning to want and avoid things so that you're never let down by what you want, and never trapped by what you're trying to avoid. He calls this the most urgent, because it's where the storms come from: grief, envy, fear, the feeling of being thwarted. They all start when a desire misses or an aversion hits. The second field is action, our impulses to do or not do: acting in order, thoughtfully, not carelessly. And here's a line that surprises people who think Stoics are cold. I'm not supposed to be unfeeling like a statue, he says. I'm supposed to keep up my relationships, the ones I was born into and the ones I chose: as a son, a brother, a father, a citizen, someone who honors the gods. The third field is assent: not being fooled, not agreeing too quickly. This one is for people already making progress, so that their judgment holds even when they're tired, or sad, or half asleep. And his warning: the philosophers of his day loved to skip straight to the third field, to clever arguments and logic puzzles, while their desires and relationships were a mess. Start where the storms start, he says. The logic can come later.

segments.voice: Hold the three fields in mind like three doors. Desire: what am I wanting or dreading today? Action: who do I owe something to, and how will I act toward them? Assent: what thought am I likely to believe too quickly? Let each door open for a few breaths, then pick one as your training field.

418.title: Found doing this
418.hook: let death find me attending to my will, Epictetus says (Discourses 3.5)
418.carry: attending to nothing but my own will
418.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners ask each morning what they would want to be found doing, and use the answer to choose how to spend part of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was three fields: desire, action and assent. Your line was let each door open for a few breaths.

I'm sick here, one of Epictetus' students says, and I want to go home. Not an unreasonable wish: if I'm going to be sick, or worse, let it be in my own bed. Epictetus answers with questions, and they lead him into a quiet passage of the Discourses, about what any of us would want to be doing when the end comes. It's less grim than it sounds.
screen: `A SICK STUDENT WANTS TO GO HOME.` → `LET IT BE IN MY OWN BED.` → `LESS GRIM THAN IT SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter five, to students who leave because of illness. Epictetus asks a few practical questions. Would you be in less danger at home? Is there no fever there? Then he widens the question. Where, and doing what, would you like death to find you? It's going to find each of us somewhere, doing something: a farmer at his farming, a trader at his trade, an official in office. Epictetus says what he would choose. Let it find me, he says, attending to nothing but my own will: keeping it calm, unhindered, unforced, free. He wants to be found practicing. And he imagines being able to say, at the end, that he used well what he'd been given: that he didn't misuse his mind, never complained of his lot, kept his commitments. That's the heart of the passage, and it isn't really about death. It's about now. If there's something you'd want to be found doing, you can be doing it already, in ordinary places. Nothing grand. Being patient with the person in front of you. Doing your work honestly. Treating your own mind with care. His answer is simple enough to carry into a kitchen or an office: whatever I'm doing, let it be something I'd be glad to be found doing.

419.title: This too trains
419.hook: how to bear a fever: this too is exercise (Discourses 3.10)
419.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners who are ill treat recovery as part of their practice: following medical care, resting, and working on patience rather than blame.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was unhindered, the will Epictetus hoped death would find calm and free. Your line was attending to nothing but my own will.

segments.voice: The thermometer beeps, and the week's plans quietly fall apart. Meetings get canceled, the to-do list sits there, and on top of feeling awful it's easy to feel useless, as if life is on pause until you're well. Epictetus knew something about bodies that don't cooperate. Ancient writers say he was lame. When he talks about illness, he isn't speaking from a healthy distance.
screen: `THE THERMOMETER BEEPS.` → `LIFE ON PAUSE.` → `ANCIENT WRITERS SAY HE WAS LAME.`

segments.voice: Discourses book three, chapter ten: how we should bear illness. It starts like a packing list. Keep your principles ready for each situation: at the table, the ones about eating; in the bath, the ones about bathing; in bed, the ones about lying in bed. And the ones about fever. A fever, he says, is part of life too, like walking, sailing or traveling. It isn't a pause. It's a different kind of practice. So what does bearing a fever well look like? He's specific. Not blaming God or other people. Not being crushed by what's happening. Doing what needs to be done. When the doctor comes in, not dreading what he'll say, and not giddy if he says you're doing well. The same things he asks on a healthy day, in a smaller room. This too is training, he says. A sick day isn't a day off from becoming who you want to be. In some ways it's a clear day for it, because the usual props are gone. You can't prove anything by being busy. You can only be patient, honest about how you feel, and kind to whoever brings the soup. This isn't a reason to ignore medicine or push through when your body needs rest. Resting well is the practice. The person lying there is still training, and still free.

420.hook: train in private: drink water in the heat and tell no one (Discourses 3.12)
420.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners keep at least one discipline entirely private, following Epictetus' advice to train for themselves rather than for an audience.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was nosos, sickness, and the fever as practice. Your line was resting well is the practice.

The ice bath video. The five a.m. run, posted at five-oh-two. The green juice and the caption about discipline. There's a whole economy now of being seen doing hard things. Some of it is genuinely inspiring. Some of it is mostly about being seen. Epictetus warned about a version of this in his own day, philosophers staging feats of endurance, and he had a test for telling the two apart.
screen: `THE ICE BATH VIDEO.` → `POSTED AT FIVE-OH-TWO.` → `A TEST TO TELL THEM APART.`

segments.voice: Discourses book three, chapter twelve, on training. First he rules things out. Don't train with stunts that are strange or showy, or philosophers will be no different from street performers. Walking a tightrope is hard and dangerous, but that's no reason to practice it. Train where it's useful: in what you want and what you avoid. Then he gets pointed. Some philosophers hugged cold statues in winter to show how tough they were; the story is told of the Cynic Diogenes. Don't, he says. If you want to train your endurance, do it for yourself, not for the people watching. Here's the exercise. When you're hot and very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. Notice: you don't even get to swallow it. The water is right there, and you let it go. A smaller version: if you've given up wine, don't go around announcing, I only drink water. The moment you announce it, part of the training can turn into a performance, and the performance takes the reward. Training in private keeps the reward in you, getting stronger. Sharing isn't always wrong. It's a test: would you still do it if no one ever knew? Look back at the week: show me one, no scorekeeping, real beauty, three fields, found doing this, this too trains. And today, privately.
screen: `NO STUNTS, NO TIGHTROPES.` · `DON'T HUG THE COLD STATUES.` · `A MOUTHFUL OF WATER, SPAT OUT.` · `WOULD YOU DO IT IF NO ONE KNEW?` · then, large: `PRIVATELY.`

segments.voice: Choose one small piece of training no one will ever see: skipping a second helping, an hour without your phone, holding back a complaint. Picture doing it, then picture the urge to mention it afterward, and let that pass too. Keep it between you and you.
Askēsis. Greek for training: Epictetus' rule for practice, no stunts, no announcements; take the cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.
Your line: privately. A mouthful of cold water, and no one told. Day four hundred twenty, and a week done.

fork.setup: you're hot and very thirsty, and you want to train your self-control. what does Epictetus suggest?
options: drink slowly, in public, so people learn from you.
take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.
go without water all day and post about it.
fork.reveal: the exercise is small, real and completely private: the reward stays in you, not in the audience.

original.note: Greek askēsis: training, exercise (our word ascetic comes from it); the subject of Discourses 3.12.

trapdoor: what you thought: discipline means doing hard things.
what it means: useful training, done privately, for yourself and not for an audience.
what a scholar hears: askēsis was also the athlete's word for training, and 3.12's target is philosophers who staged endurance feats, like hugging statues in winter, a habit told of Diogenes.
recall: a little book kept in the hand

chat.says: I'm doing a cold-shower challenge. Should I post it every day to stay motivated?
options: Maybe keep some of it private. Epictetus warns showing off can steal the reward.
Yes. Epictetus says training only counts when other people can see it.
No. Epictetus says any hard training is a stunt and should be dropped.
chat.meaning: Epictetus says train for yourself, not for watchers: spit out the cold water and tell no one. Announcing it can turn training into performance.

Diogenes.meaning: a Cynic philosopher said to have hugged cold statues in winter

Cynic.meaning: a follower of a Greek school that lived on almost nothing

Discourses.meaning: Arrian's record of Epictetus' talks, in four books
